summary: Nahum 2 portrays an attack on Nineveh in rapid scenes: commands to defend the fortress, flashing chariots, stumbling troops, opened river gates, and a palace collapsing. The chapter then pictures the city fleeing, being plundered, and becoming “empty, void, and waste.” It ends by turning Nineveh into a lion’s den whose power is cut off by Yahweh of Armies.
whyItMatters: This chapter is the book’s central siege poem, showing the downfall of the Assyrian capital as relief for Jacob and Israel. It also forces readers to face the chapter’s violent images while recognizing that the poem is directed against a predatory imperial power.

context.author: The heading of the book attributes the vision to Nahum the Elkoshite, but gives no biography and does not identify the final arranger of the book.
context.audience: Judah is addressed with news of relief in the book, while Nineveh and Assyrian power are the main targets of the poems.
context.date: Commonly set between the Assyrian sack of Thebes in 663 BCE and Nineveh’s fall in 612 BCE, though the book gives no exact date for composition or final arrangement.
context.setting: The poems concern Judah and Nineveh, the Assyrian imperial capital in northern Mesopotamia, in the seventh-century BCE world of Assyria and Judah.
context.literaryForm: Prophetic poetry with siege scenes, taunts, vivid commands, animal imagery, and speeches presented as Yahweh’s words.

outline.heading: Defend the fortress
outline.note: The chapter opens with urgent defensive commands, then explains the scene in relation to Yahweh restoring Jacob and Israel after destroyers have ruined them.

outline.heading: Battle rushes through the streets
outline.note: Red shields, scarlet-clad warriors, flashing chariots, rushing movement, and stumbling picked troops compress the battle into quick images.

outline.heading: The city gives way
outline.note: River gates open, the palace dissolves, and a female figure is uncovered and carried away while servants mourn.

outline.heading: Flight and plunder
outline.note: Nineveh, once like a pool of water, empties as people flee; the city’s silver, gold, and treasure are taken, leaving terror and waste.

outline.heading: The lions’ den is silenced
outline.note: The poem asks where the lions’ den has gone, recalls its stored prey, and closes with Yahweh’s direct threat to burn chariots, cut off prey, and silence messengers.

keyVerses.text: For Yahweh restores the excellency of Jacob as the excellency of Israel, for the destroyers have destroyed them and ruined their vine branches.
keyVerses.why: This verse gives the siege scene its larger frame: Nineveh’s downfall is connected to restoration for Jacob and Israel after destruction.

keyVerses.text: The gates of the rivers are opened, and the palace is dissolved.
keyVerses.why: The line marks the collapse of the city’s defenses and royal center in one compact image.

keyVerses.text: She is empty, void, and waste. The heart melts, the knees knock together, their bodies and faces have grown pale.
keyVerses.why: This verse gathers the result of the plunder into a stark picture of desolation and fear.

keyVerses.text: “Behold, I am against you,” says Yahweh of Armies, “and I will burn her chariots in the smoke, and the sword will devour your young lions; and I will cut off your prey from the earth, and the voice of your messengers will no longer be heard.”
keyVerses.why: The chapter’s final word is presented as Yahweh’s direct speech against the city and its predatory power.

questions.question: Who is the chapter speaking to at the beginning?
questions.answer: The opening commands address the threatened city as an attacker comes against it. Nineveh is named in verse 8, so the defensive commands are best read within the chapter’s portrayal of Nineveh under siege. The poem does not pause to identify every speaker or military actor by name.

questions.question: Why does verse 2 mention Jacob and Israel in a chapter about Nineveh?
questions.answer: In WEB, verse 2 connects Nineveh’s defeat with Yahweh restoring the excellency of Jacob and Israel after destroyers have ruined them. Other editions phrase the action differently: KJV has turned away, and Brenton 2:3 has turned aside. The restoration language followed here belongs to WEB. Brenton places the chapter boundary differently, so its numbers do not align exactly with WEB’s throughout chapter 2.

questions.question: What does “fortress” mean here?
questions.answer: In verse 1, “fortress” is part of a string of commands: “Keep the fortress! Watch the way! Strengthen your waist! Fortify your power mightily!” The word points to the defended city or stronghold under attack. The line sounds urgent because the commands come after the one who “dashes in pieces” has come up against the addressee.

questions.question: Are the chariots described as attackers or defenders?
questions.answer: The chapter does not label every chariot with a side. Verses 3-4 describe shields, warriors, chariots, and spears in fast battle imagery, while verse 5 speaks of troops dashing to the wall. Readers should be cautious about turning these poetic snapshots into a detailed military diagram.

questions.question: Do “the gates of the rivers” explain exactly how Nineveh fell?
questions.answer: Verse 6 says the river gates are opened and the palace is dissolved. That gives a powerful image of collapse, but the line by itself does not supply an engineering report or a full siege chronology. The chapter is prophetic poetry, not a technical account of the city’s capture.

questions.question: Who is the woman in verse 7?
questions.answer: WEB presents an unnamed feminine figure who is uncovered, carried away, and mourned by servants. The city personified or its royal dignity may be in view, but the identification is uncertain. KJV prints Huzzab where WEB begins with a decree; that disputed expression does not establish the biography of a queen. Brenton 2:8 begins with an exposed foundation before the captivity imagery, another difference to notice when comparing editions.

questions.question: Why compare Nineveh to a pool of water?
questions.answer: Verse 8 says Nineveh has long been “like a pool of water,” but then people flee away. The image contrasts stored, gathered stability with sudden draining and panic. The shouted “Stop! Stop!” fails because no one looks back.

questions.question: What is the point of the lions in verses 11-13?
questions.answer: The lion imagery pictures Nineveh as a powerful predator’s den, a place where prey was safely stored and no one made the lions afraid. Verse 13 reverses that image: Yahweh says he will cut off the prey, burn the chariots, and silence the messengers. The metaphor connects imperial power with predation and then imagines that power removed.

questions.question: Does the chapter celebrate violence without reservation?
questions.answer: The chapter portrays violent reversal against Nineveh and presents Yahweh as opposing the city. Its statement about restoring Jacob and Israel connects the siege to relief after oppression. That political purpose does not remove the violence of the plunder and humiliation scenes; readers can attend both to the promised relief and to the suffering the poem depicts.

glossary.def: A defended stronghold or city position. In this chapter it is what the addressee is urgently commanded to keep as the attack begins.
War vehicles that dominate the battle imagery in verses 3-4 and return in Yahweh’s threat in verse 13.
Goods seized from a defeated city. Verse 9 names silver and gold as plunder, then says there is an abundance of precious treasure.
What a predator takes. The chapter uses it in the lion image for Nineveh’s accumulated spoils, then says Yahweh will cut it off from the earth.
